q: How large a quantity of heat is needed when 2.0 kg of water is heated from 15 °C to 65 °C ($c = 4190\,\tfrac{\text{J}}{\text{kg}\cdot\text{K}}$)?
A kilogram of water and a kilogram of iron receive the same quantity of heat in a sauna. Whose temperature rises more, and about how many times as much?
a: The iron's. Its specific heat capacity, 450 J/(kg·K), is about one ninth of that of water, 4190 J/(kg·K), so the same quantity of heat raises the temperature of the iron about nine times as much.

q: Equal amounts of 80-degree and 20-degree water are mixed in an insulated container. What is the final temperature, and why does the answer not hold if there is three times as much hot water?
a: 50 °C, because the masses and the substance are the same, and the heat given out is equal to the heat received. If there is three times as much hot water, the equilibrium is closer to 80 °C (65 °C), because the heat capacity of the hot water is three times as large.
